09-21.label: Daily Lectionary
09-21.verse: “The fool says in his heart, ‘There is no God.’”
09-21.heading: Who may dwell on the holy hill?
paragraphs: Psalm 14 opens bluntly: the fool says in his heart there is no God. But the verse isn't really about atheism as an opinion — it's a diagnosis. God looks down to see if anyone is wise, anyone seeking him, and the verdict is stark: all have turned aside, there is no one who does good, not even one. It isn't a psalm about bad people out there somewhere. It's a psalm about the human condition, full stop.

Psalm 15 asks the natural follow-up question: LORD, who may dwell in your tent? Who may live on your holy mountain? And it answers with a list — walk blamelessly, speak truth, don't slander a neighbor, keep your word even when it costs you. Read back to back, the two psalms set an impossible bar right next to a diagnosis that says no one clears it.

That tension isn't a flaw in the psalms — it's the point. The Law draws the shape of a righteous life precisely so we stop pretending we can climb it under our own strength. What Psalm 15 demands, only grace can supply.

confession.quote: Also they teach that since the fall of Adam all men begotten in the natural way are born with sin, that is, without the fear of God, without trust in God, and with concupiscence…
confession.cite: Augsburg Confession, Article II — Of Original Sin

09-22.label: Daily Lectionary
09-22.verse: “Preserve me, O God, for in you I take refuge… I have no good apart from you.”
09-22.heading: No good apart from you
paragraphs: Psalm 16 opens as a prayer of refuge, then makes a striking claim: I have no good apart from you. Not "you're one good thing among several" — the only good there is. Everything else the psalm lists, the good company, the pleasant inheritance, flows from that one relationship rather than sitting alongside it.

Psalm 17 asks for the same refuge under a harder pressure: enemies who trust their own strength and their "portion in this life." Against that, the psalmist asks to be kept "as the apple of the eye," hidden "in the shadow of your wings" — and closes with an odd kind of confidence: satisfied, it says, just by beholding God's presence. Not rescued and moving on to something else. Satisfied by the presence itself.
Both psalms describe a trust that has nowhere else to go. That isn't weakness dressed up as piety — it's just an honest description of what it actually means to have no other god before this one.

confession.quote: We should fear, love, and trust in God above all things.
confession.cite: Small Catechism, The Ten Commandments — The First Commandment

10-28.label: Daily Lectionary
10-28.verse: "Make haste, O God, to deliver me! Make haste to help me, O LORD!"
10-28.heading: Make Haste, O God, to Help
paragraphs: Psalm 70 doesn't ease into prayer -- it opens with a cry for rescue, repeated almost word for word from the end of Psalm 40. David isn't interested in polished phrases. He's drowning, enemies are circling, and he needs God now, not eventually. There's something honest and almost uncomfortable about a prayer this urgent -- most of us have been taught to compose ourselves before we approach God. David skips that step entirely.

Then Psalm 71 picks up the same desperation but stretches it out over a whole life. Here the voice is older -- 'do not cast me off in the time of old age' -- looking back at a God who has been faithful since birth and pleading for that faithfulness to hold to the very end. The psalmist doesn't claim to have earned this care. He simply remembers it, and remembering becomes the grounds for asking again.

Both psalms refuse to let us believe that faith means never being desperate. They hand us words for the moments when we have no other words -- when all we can say is hurry, Lord, help me, don't leave me now. And the promise underneath both psalms is the same one we cling to in every crisis: God does not require us to get our prayers right before He turns His ear. He hears the cry itself, and He comes.

confession.quote: We should fear, love, and trust in God above all things.
confession.cite: Small Catechism, The Ten Commandments — The First Commandment

10-30.label: Daily Lectionary
10-30.verse: "Yet God my King is from of old, working salvation in the midst of the earth."
10-30.heading: Remember, O Lord, and Rise Up
paragraphs: Psalm 74 is a cry from the ruins. The sanctuary is smoke, the enemy has set up his own standards where God's people once worshiped, and the psalmist asks the question every suffering believer eventually asks: why have you cast us off forever? There's no pretending here, no forced smile. The psalm simply lays the wreckage in front of God and says, look at this. How long?

But right in the middle of the complaint, something shifts. The psalmist remembers -- you divided the sea, you crushed the heads of the sea monsters, you fixed the sun and moon, you established the boundaries of the earth. The appeal isn't to God's sympathy but to his character and his track record. He has always been the one who works salvation in the midst of the earth, not from a safe distance. That memory doesn't erase the ruins, but it gives the complaint somewhere to stand.

Psalm 75 answers almost like morning after that long night: we give thanks, for your name is near. God himself sets the time for judgment; he is the one who brings down the proud and lifts up the humble, holding the cup of justice in his own hand. The two psalms together teach something very Lutheran -- faith doesn't deny the ruins or demand we feel differently than we do, but it keeps calling on the God who has always been near, long before we could see it.

confession.quote: God would thereby tenderly urge us to believe that He is our true Father, and that we are His true children, so that we may ask Him confidently with all assurance, as dear children ask their dear father.
confession.cite: Small Catechism, The Lord's Prayer — Introduction

10-31.label: Daily Lectionary
10-31.verse: "I will remember the deeds of the LORD; yes, I will remember your wonders of old."
10-31.heading: Remembering God's Mighty Deeds
paragraphs: Psalm 76 opens with God known and feared in Judah, his tent in Zion, his power breaking the flashing arrows, the shield, the sword, and the weapons of war. This is a picture of a God who doesn't need our help defending his people -- when he rises to judgment, the earth itself goes quiet and still. It's the kind of security that makes human might look small, because it is.

Then the evening reading turns the camera around. Psalm 77 is not a song of confident triumph but of a soul in trouble, crying aloud to God in the night, wondering if his steadfast love has run dry, if his promises have failed. Anyone who has lain awake rehearsing their fears knows this psalm. The turn doesn't come from the psalmist finding a new argument or a burst of willpower -- it comes from memory.

"I will remember the deeds of the LORD," he says, and starts recounting the exodus, the sea, the ancient wonders. That's the move for us too, in our own sleepless nights: not to manufacture feelings of faith, but to remember what God has actually done -- supremely in Christ crucified and risen. Our trust isn't self-generated; it rests on deeds already accomplished for us, which is why we can say with the Catechism that we are to fear, love, and trust in God above all things.

confession.quote: We should fear, love, and trust in God above all things.
confession.cite: Small Catechism, The Ten Commandments — The First Commandment

11-03.label: Daily Lectionary
11-03.verse: "I have laid upon you the years of their iniquity... you shall bear the sin of the house of Israel."
11-03.heading: Bearing the Weight of Israel's Sin
paragraphs: God tells Ezekiel to lie on his side, bound with cords, acting out the siege of Jerusalem in his own body. For over a year he bears the weight of Israel's sin pressed into his flesh -- a living sign nobody could ignore. It's a strange and uncomfortable chapter, and it's meant to be. This isn't theater; it's judgment made visible, so the people could see what their rebellion actually costs.

Chapter 5 turns from sign to sentence. Jerusalem, set in the center of the nations, has become worse than the nations around her -- she has rejected the very statutes God gave for life. The famine, the sword, the scattering: none of it is arbitrary cruelty. It's the slow unraveling of a people who trusted everything except the God who made and kept them.

Here's the strange mercy underneath the wreckage: God doesn't look away from what sin costs, and neither does he hide it from us. He lets Ezekiel carry it visibly so that we might finally see our own iniquity named, not excused. The weight Ezekiel bore in picture, Christ bore in full -- not as a sign pointing elsewhere, but as the sin-bearer himself, so that the siege against us would end at the cross and not at our own ruin.

confession.quote: Also they teach that since the fall of Adam all men begotten in the natural way are born with sin, that is, without the fear of God, without trust in God, and with concupiscence…
confession.cite: Augsburg Confession, Article II — Of Original Sin

11-04.label: Daily Lectionary
11-04.verse: "Then shall ye know that I am the LORD."
11-04.heading: The Mountains Will Know the Lord
paragraphs: Ezekiel 6 is a word against the high places -- those hills and altars where Israel had set up idols, mixing worship of the true God with whatever else seemed useful at the time. God doesn't negotiate with this. The mountains themselves are addressed, the altars are named for destruction, and the refrain lands again and again: "then shall ye know that I am the LORD." Not a gentle correction. A leveling.

Chapter 7 presses the point further. "An end, the end is come" -- the day has arrived, and no amount of silver or gold will buy anyone out of it. Judgment isn't delayed because people have run out of excuses; it comes because the idolatry has run its course. There's a strange mercy hidden even here: God names what's false so that what's left, however little, is true.

We don't usually bow to carved images, but we know what it is to build our own high places -- the things we trust to hold us up when God himself feels distant or demanding. The first commandment doesn't just forbid statues; it claims the whole heart. Fear, love, and trust belong to God above all things, not because he's jealous for no reason, but because everything else we trust will eventually be torn down, and he alone remains to be known.

confession.quote: We should fear, love, and trust in God above all things.
confession.cite: Small Catechism, The Ten Commandments — The First Commandment

11-05.label: Daily Lectionary
11-05.verse: "Son of man, have you seen what the elders of the house of Israel are doing in the dark, each in his room of pictures?"
11-05.heading: Idols in the Dark, Mercy on the Mark
paragraphs: Ezekiel is given a vision tour of the temple, and it's worse than anyone imagined. Behind closed doors, in rooms carved with idols, the elders of Israel are burning incense to images and telling themselves God doesn't see -- "the LORD has forsaken the land." The irony is brutal: the very people charged with guarding God's house have filled it with everything but God. Chapter 9 answers that secret worship with a terrifying visitation -- a man with a writing kit marks the foreheads of those who grieve over the sin, and judgment falls on everyone else, beginning at the sanctuary itself.

We don't burn incense to carved beasts, but we know what it is to keep a private room of pictures -- the places in our hearts we assume God can't see, where we've quietly set up something else to trust, fear, or love more than him. Ezekiel's vision strips away the comfortable fiction that worship is only what happens in public. God sees the whole house, every room, including the ones we've locked.

And yet the mark in chapter 9 is mercy before it is judgment -- a sign placed on those who mourn their sin, protecting them precisely because they have stopped pretending. That's the pattern grace always takes: not denial, not bargaining, but honest grief over what's true, met by a God who marks his own for safekeeping. The temple may be defiled, but the One who marks still saves.

confession.quote: Of Repentance they teach that for those who have fallen after Baptism there is remission of sins whenever they are converted, and that the Church ought to impart absolution to those thus returning to repentance... They also are rejected who do not teach that remission of sins comes through faith but command us to merit grace through satisfactions of our own.
confession.cite: Augsburg Confession, Article XII — Of Repentance
